newsitem.title: UK: Labour says IRA truce needed for N.Irish progress.
newsitem.headline: Labour says IRA truce needed for N.Irish progress.

text.p: Mo Mowlam, the woman tipped to be Northern Ireland Secretary in a new British government elected on Friday, said IRA guerrillas must call a truce before their Sinn Fein political wing is given a place in peace talks.

Mowlam, one of the victors in a landslide Labour win that installed Tony Blair as new British leader, said there would be no change in its refusal to talk with Sinn Fein while Irish Republican Army fighters were on a war footing.

"We have made it very clear that none of my colleagues will have any contact with Sinn Fein while the IRA makes that impossible. However there is a door open there and they know the conditions through which they will facilitate others to pass through it," she said in a BBC radio interview.

Mitchel McLaughlin, chairman of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, said his party would "approach this new government and the opportunity to rebuild the peace process with flexibility and imagination,and I hope that is reciprocated".
McLaughlin, speaking minutes before counting for Northern Ireland's 18 parliamentary seats got under way, said the peace process could be restored if Mowlam showed new flexibility.

"I believe if she...hits the ground running...then it can all be put together again, because I believe that all the necessary component parts are still on the table, even if somewhat askew...I genuinely believe that we are looking at a new opportunity for peace."

Irish Deputy Prime Minister Dick Spring, one of the architects of a three-year Anglo-Irish peace drive thrown into disarray by resurgent Irish Republican Army guerrillas, applauded Blair's accession to power and said he would have Northern Ireland talks with him and Mowlam next week.
Spring was confident that Northern Ireland would be a priority for Blair and he urged flexibility on all sides to resolve the region's deep-seated problems.
Spring said the two Labour parties were members of the European Parliament's Socialist Group, and he hailed Blair's success "as a great victory".
"There is a new government and it has a huge mandate and, as I see it, it behoves them to take up the baton in relation to Northern Ireland," Spring told BBC radio.

Referring to earlier comments by McLaughlin, Spring said: "I heard words like flexibility and imagination being used. We all need to have flexibility and imagination. We also all need to have generosity with one another if we are going solve the problems of Northern Ireland.
"But Tony Blair has a very strong majority and I know that he will have Northern Ireland very high on his agenda...98% of the people want a peaceful resolution of this conflict."
Sinn Fein accused Blair's predecessor John Major of driving peace efforts into the ground by refusing it a place in peace talks during a 17 month IRA ceasefire.
The IRA says it will not call a truce until republicans are given a date for admission to fresh all-party negotiations.

In the last days of the campaign, Blair pledged that a Labour government would not be cowed by IRA violence and that Britain would not give in to bombs like those the IRA set off on mainland Britain in the runup to polling day.
